title: Predict the output: a loop that adds i to a List<Short> and then removes the last element whenever size > 1 — what prints and why?
shortTitle: Predict output — loop adding to List<Short> with removal — autoboxing trap

s1_definition.profdef: This is an AUTOBOXING trap. `List<Short>` stores Short objects. `list.add((short) i)` boxes `short` to `Short`. But `list.remove(i)` where `i` is an `int` calls `remove(int index)` (remove by INDEX), NOT `remove(Short)` (remove by OBJECT). The `int` parameter matches the overload `remove(int index)` which removes at position `i`. This causes unexpected behavior: the removal is by index, not by value.
s1_definition.analogy: You add cheque #1, #2, #3 to a box. You say "remove 1" — did you mean remove cheque #1 (by value) or remove the cheque at position 1 (by index)? Java picks "by index" when the argument is int, "by value" when it's Short/Integer object. This ambiguity causes the surprise.
s1_definition.oneliner: list.remove(int) = remove by INDEX. list.remove(Object) = remove by VALUE. When i is int, remove(i) calls the index overload. Cast to (Short) for value removal.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is an AUTOBOXING trap. `List<Short>` stores Short objects. `list.add((short) i)` boxes `short` to `Short`. But `list.remove(i)` where `i` is an `int` calls `remove(int index)` (remove by INDEX), NOT `remove(Short)` (remove by OBJECT). The `int` parameter matches the overload `remove(int index)` which removes at position `i`. This causes unexpected behavior: the removal is by index, not by value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** You add cheque #1, #2, #3 to a box. You say "remove 1" — did you mean remove cheque #1 (by value) or remove the cheque at position 1 (by index)? Java picks "by index" when the argument is int, "by value" when it's Short/Integer object. This ambiguity causes the surprise.

**One line to remember:** list.remove(int) = remove by INDEX. list.remove(Object) = remove by VALUE. When i is int, remove(i) calls the index overload. Cast to (Short) for value removal.

sections.s2_technical:
This puzzle exposes the `List.remove` overload trap combined with autoboxing. `List<Short>` has two `remove` methods: `remove(int index)` removes by position, and `remove(Object o)` removes by value. When you call `list.remove(1)`, the literal `1` is an `int`, so Java picks `remove(int index)` — it removes the element at index 1, NOT the Short value 1.

To remove by VALUE you must pass an object: `list.remove(Short.valueOf((short) 1))` or `list.remove((Short) (short) 1)`. Autoboxing does not happen for overload selection here because an exact `int` overload exists and is preferred over boxing to `Object`. This is why a loop that expects to delete values ends up deleting by index and shifting elements unexpectedly.

A banking example: a list of short settlement codes is pruned in a loop; calling `remove(code)` where `code` is an `int` silently deletes the wrong element and corrupts the batch. Senior nuance: prefer `removeIf(c -> c == target)` or explicit boxing to make value-removal unambiguous; never rely on an `int` literal when the list element type is a boxed number.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A batch job pruned short settlement codes with `list.remove(1)`, expecting to delete the value 1 but actually deleting the element at index 1, corrupting the batch. Fix: pass a boxed `Short.valueOf((short) 1)` (or use `removeIf`) so the `remove(Object)` overload runs and the correct value is removed.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: two identical lists [10, 20, 30] of Short.

**Step 2.** `byIndex.remove(1)` — the literal 1 is an int, so `remove(int index)` runs and deletes the element at index 1, which is 20.

**Step 3.** `byValue.remove(Short.valueOf((short) 10))` passes an Object, so `remove(Object)` runs and deletes the VALUE 10.

**Step 4.** Same syntax shape, opposite outcome — the overload chosen depends on whether the argument is a primitive int or a boxed Short.

**Step 5.** byIndex becomes [10, 30]; byValue becomes [20, 30].

```text
INFO: byIndex=[10, 30] byValue=[20, 30]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  list.remove(2)                → remove(int index) → removes element at position 2
  list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) → remove(Object)   → removes first occurrence of value 2
  list.remove((Integer) 2)      → remove(Object)    → removes first occurrence of value 2

  THE TRAP:
  short i = 2;
  list.remove(i);  → short widened to int → remove(int index) → removes at position 2!
  list.remove(Short.valueOf(i)); → remove(Object) → removes value 2!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  remove() Overload Resolution (Cheque Batch List)          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  List<Short> chequeIds  (holds Short objects)              │
│        │                                                   │
│        ▼                                                   │
│  list.remove(i)  where i is int/short                      │
│        │                                                   │
│        ├─ int arg  ──► remove(int index)  ◄── BY INDEX     │
│        │                (removes position i — the trap)    │
│        └─ Object arg ─► remove(Object o)  ◄── BY VALUE     │
│                         (list.remove(Short.valueOf(i)))    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Buggy code (remove cheque id by value, intended)         │
│───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ List<Short> ids = new ArrayList<>();                     │
│ for (short i=0;i<5;i++) ids.add(i);  // [0,1,2,3,4]       │
│ ids.remove((short) 3);                                   │
│   // short widens to int → remove(int index)             │
│   // removes element AT index 3 (value 3 here by luck)   │
│ ids.remove(10);  // IndexOutOfBounds (no value match!)   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Correct removal by value                                 │
│───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ ids.remove(Short.valueOf((short) 3)); // remove(Object)  │
│   → removes the element whose VALUE is 3                 │
│ // same trap on List<Integer>:                           │
│ List<Integer> amts = ...;                                │
│ amts.remove(i);              // BY INDEX  (trap)         │
│ amts.remove(Integer.valueOf(i)); // BY VALUE (correct)   │
│ Rule: primitive arg → index overload; box it for value  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The autoboxing trap: `List.remove(int)` removes by INDEX, `List.remove(Object)` removes by VALUE. When the argument is a primitive int or short (widened to int), Java calls the index overload. To remove by value, explicitly box: `list.remove(Short.valueOf(i))` or `list.remove((Integer) i)`. This is a classic interview trick — the interviewer shows code using `list.remove(i)` with an int loop variable on a `List<Integer>` and asks "what happens?" The answer: it removes by index, not by value.
